Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES

At 18 Marlowe Court, a six-storey apartment building in Northbridge, residents began reporting intermittent trouble with the front-door intercom in early October. The system still rang in most apartments, but some calls ended before anyone could answer. Building manager Lena Ortiz first heard about the problem from two residents on October 4. She logged their reports separately because one lived on the second floor and the other on the fifth, and they did not describe exactly the same symptoms.

The first resident, Mr. Kwan in apartment 2C, said that the lobby panel rang his handset once and then went quiet. He told Lena, “I can hear the first buzz, but when I lift the receiver, there’s nothing.” The second resident, Anika Bell in 5A, said her handset sometimes worked after she pressed the door-release button, even when nobody had called. Lena noted that as her observation, not as a confirmed fault in the release circuit. Neither resident reported being unable to open the building door with a key.

Lena checked the call log and found that complaints had also been made on September 28 and October 1, but the earlier notes did not name apartments. The concierge, Tomas Reed, recalled that a delivery driver had waited outside for several minutes on September 30 because no one answered the panel. He could not confirm whether the call had reached any apartment. Lena added his recollection to the building file with the date he gave, rather than treating it as a verified system test.

A technician from Bellwether Access, Priya Shah, visited on October 8. She tested the lobby panel with Lena and checked handsets in 2C and 5A. The panel’s display and call buttons appeared normal during the visit, and both handsets rang when she placed test calls. The test did not reproduce the reported cutout. Priya said, “It may be a loose connection, but I haven’t found one yet.” She asked Lena to keep a record of the next failures, including the apartment number and approximate time.

On October 10, Lena and Tomas looked at the wiring cabinet in the basement. Its door was closed but not latched; there was no sign of damage to the lock. Tomas said a contractor had used the corridor earlier that week, though he did not know whether that person had opened the cabinet. Lena photographed the cabinet and its visible labels. She did not open or adjust the wiring. The building file records the cabinet’s condition as observed that morning and does not identify who last accessed it.

The next reported failure came from 2C at about 7:20 p.m. on October 12. Mr. Kwan said the handset rang, then the sound stopped when he picked it up. Lena called the apartment from the lobby panel shortly afterward; that test worked. Bellwether Access scheduled a return visit for October 16. Lena asked residents to continue using their keys if the intercom failed and to contact the concierge if a visitor was waiting outside. She did not tell residents that the system was fixed or that the reports had stopped.

1. Return visit and observed work

Priya arrived at 9:15 a.m. on October 16 and repeated the lobby-to-apartment tests. She also checked the terminal connections in the basement cabinet and found one screw terminal that was not as tight as the adjacent terminals. She tightened it and marked the connection with a small paint line so a later inspection could show whether it had shifted. Priya said this was a possible cause of the intermittent calls, but she could not establish that it explained every report. She did not replace the panel, handsets, or wiring.

After the adjustment, Priya placed three test calls to 2C and three to 5A. All six calls rang, and the residents could speak with her from their handsets. Lena watched the tests and recorded the results. Priya also pressed the door-release control once during a test with Lena present; the lobby door released. This was a limited check during the visit, not a guarantee about later operation. The technician left at 10:05 a.m. and advised Lena to note any further interruption before requesting another visit.

That evening, Anika Bell told Lena that a call had come through normally at about 6:40 p.m. She did not know who had called. On October 18, Mr. Kwan reported that his handset had worked for two calls that day, one from a relative and one from the concierge. Lena wrote down what he reported without independently checking those calls. No resident had yet reported another cutout after the October 16 visit, but Lena planned to keep the log open through the end of the month.

The repair invoice, received on October 19, listed an inspection and tightening of a terminal connection; it did not list replacement parts. Bellwether Access charged for the scheduled return visit, and Lena filed the invoice with the technician’s service notes. The building’s maintenance budget had enough remaining in its intercom line to cover this visit. If another interruption occurs before October 31, Lena will send Bellwether the dated log and ask whether a further diagnostic visit is needed.
